newsitem.title: USA: AWAY ON BUSINESS: Carry-on woes.
newsitem.headline: AWAY ON BUSINESS: Carry-on woes.

text.p: The increasingly crowded conditions faced by air travelers have forced some carriers to play hardball with passengers trying to board with carry-on luggage big enough for a kitchen sink.
Some strictly enforce the two-item rule; others specify the size and request travelers to check anything that doesn't fit in a skeletal frame or box at the check-in counter.
But the situation varies widely. Often enforcement is lax and the results unpleasant. One reader reports:

"I am in the minority I do not try to carry on three-suiter suit cases and I wish the airlines and the Federal Aviation Administration would get serious about enforcing the bag size and quantity (rules).
"I travel about 30,000 miles per year and am getting tired of sitting in my aisle seat and getting assulted by the large suit cases being dragged down the aisle.
"I am also tired of boarding late and not finding room for my coat and brief case because someone carries on all of their worldly possessions."
Lucky you, some would respond, for even snaring an aisle seat these days.

Of course if you travelled, say, 100,000 miles a year you'd no doubt be eligible for one of the elevated frequent flier levels that allows you to board early -- and get first crack at the overhead bin space before the rest of the passengers.
One frequent flier whose travel fell off drastically tells us that he suffered from withdrawal from perks like that one, along with upgrades and the like.
There is no easy solution to the carry-on problem other than throwing your business to carriers who are serious about enforcing the rules, and complaining to those who don't.
There is every indication that crowded conditions in the air are here to stay.
Runzheimer International, a Wisconsin-based management consulting firm, had made a projection through the year 2002 which predicts little abatement in business travel demand.
International travel will make up an even larger proportion of the mix than it does today, the forecast said.

A final note on carry-on bags. Smart Money magazine, which is published by the Wall Street Journal, reports in its February issue that it has found the perfect carry-on bag -- the Hartmann Deluxe Mobile Traveller.

It's a 10-pound affair that is 14 inches wide, 22 inches high and 10 inches deep. Perfection does carry a price -- $495 in this case. The bag is equipped with wheels and a pull-out handle that extends to 38 inches, the magazine reports.
